None of Nithya Raman’s council colleagues backed her bid for mayor. Will they work with her?
Aaron Schrank
has been on the ground, reporting on homelessness and other issues in L.A. for more than a decade.
Published November 6, 2026 at 5:00 AM PST
Updated November 6, 2026 at 10:30 AM PST
City Council members from left, Tim McOsker, Eunisses Hernandez, Nithya Raman and Marqueece Harris-Dawson at an L.A. City Council meeting.
Brian van der Brug
Getty Images)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
Raman and the City Council
The view from the progressive bloc
What Raman’s critics say
What challenges lie ahead
Positioning for Raman's replacement on the council
Nithya Raman won the race for Los Angeles mayor this week and unseated incumbent Karen Bass without a single endorsement from her colleagues on the City Council.
She won without them, but she’ll have to govern with them.
Raman, a two-term councilmember and member of the Democratic Socialists of America, entered the race in February just hours before the filing deadline and shortly after endorsing Bass. The move caught some colleagues off guard and angered Bass allies, who noted the mayor had helped Raman win reelection two years ago.
After Bass conceded Thursday, nearly every councilmember said they were ready to work with Mayor-elect Raman, who takes office on Dec. 14.
In a video message Thursday, she spoke to Angelenos who voted for Bass or skipped the election altogether.
“I am going to City Hall to work every single day to earn your trust, and to earn your trust in this city again,” Raman said.
She’ll also have to win support from a council that backed her opponent.
Sponsored message
Thirteen of the 14 endorsed Bass, including other DSA-affiliated councilmembers.
How Raman gets along with the council will shape whether she can deliver on her campaign promises. She has pledged to reduce the number of people living in tents and encampments by at least 50% before the 2028 Olympics, triple annual housing construction and staff a film office in the mayor's office to win back Hollywood jobs.
The council approves the city budget, confirms the mayor’s appointees and will decide who fills Raman’s own council seat.
Councilmember Hugo Soto-Martínez, right, speaks with Councilmember Nithya Raman at City Hall.
Genaro Molina
Getty Images)
"Although the mayor has a lot of power, much of the legislation and action items are going to have to go through [the] council,” Councilmember Hugo Soto-Martínez, another DSA-affiliated councilmember, told LAist Thursday.
“I'm looking forward to working with her on these issues, but just from a different perspective,” Soto-Martínez continued. “There are moments where we might not be on the same page, as with this mayoral campaign, but there's a lot that we agree on.”
LAist asked the 12 members of L.A.'s City Council who will serve alongside Raman how they plan to work with her. (Councilmembers Bob Blumenfield and Curren Price are leaving the council.) All but one responded or posted congratulations online.
Sponsored message
Most pledged to partner with her on basic city services: working streetlights, fixed sidewalks, help for renters.
“Of course, there’s going to be disagreement,” Councilmember Katy Yaroslavsky told LAist. “The entire body supported the incumbent. Disagreement is inevitable, but dysfunction is a choice, and we do not have the luxury right now of dysfunction. We need to come together and govern.”
Some warned that the job ahead won't be easy.
“We have many challenges ahead of us,” said Councilmember Adrin Nazarian, in a statement provided to LAist. “And I trust that Mayor-elect Raman is ready to face them head-on.”
The view from the progressive bloc
Councilmembers Eunisses Hernandez and Ysabel Jurado — both DSA members like Raman — endorsed Bass in May. Soto-Martínez had also backed Bass before Raman entered the race.
On Thursday, all three welcomed Raman’s win. Hernandez told LAist in a statement that she and Raman already have a track record of passing progressive policies together. Those included coauthoring the Sanctuary City Ordinance and advancing stronger protections for tenants facing eviction and harassment.
Sponsored message
“We’ve shown what's possible when we challenge the status quo, and I'm excited about what we can accomplish together with her in the Mayor's Office,” Hernandez wrote.
Jurado, who chairs the committee focused on homelessness, said the city of L.A. needs to deliver affordable housing, safer streets, pathways out of homelessness and reliable city services.
"Mayor-elect Raman will have a committed partner in me as we take on that work,” Jurado said in a statement. “We share a belief that working people should be able to build a future in this city, and I am ready to work alongside her to make that promise real for more Angelenos.”
Soto-Martínez said he and Raman talked after she entered the race and knew they’d be on opposite sides. But he said the issues Raman talked about during her campaign are important to the district he represents — which includes Hollywood, East Hollywood and parts of Northeast L.A.
“My district is about 83% renters, and we have about 700 people a month who get a notice of eviction for non-payment of rent,” Soto-Martínez told LAist. “And so I look forward to working on the affordability crisis and making sure that tenants stay indoors.”
He said he looks forward to the next chapter, with Raman as mayor.

is closely covering this year’s elections.
Published November 5, 2026 at 3:53 PM PST
Updated November 6, 2026 at 11:42 AM PST
Marissa Roy has won the race for Los Angeles city attorney.
Courtesy of the Marissa Roy campaign)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
Topline:
Marissa Roy will be the next L.A. city attorney. Her opponent, John McKinney, has conceded.
How we got here: Roy held on to a strong lead over McKinney ever since polls closed and is currently ahead by more than twice as many votes. Roy will be a fresh face to the role after the incumbent city attorney, Hydee Feldstein Soto, was ousted in the June primary in a rare defeat of an elected city official.
What the candidates had to say:
Roy told LAist Friday that her campaign built  a wide coalition of Angelenos who believe that the city attorney can be a powerful fighter for the people.  "We are going to use that coalition to start building cases," she said. "We've been spending the last 19 months talking to people about what they've been facing ... and now we are going to start working with the attorneys to put some of that into action. People can start expecting the justice they asked for."
McKinney said in a statement that while the results are not what he hoped for, "I accept the outcome and congratulate Marissa Roy on her victory. I wish her well as she prepares to serve as Los Angeles City Attorney. Her success in protecting our residents and serving the public interest will be important to the future of our city."
What’s at stake: The city attorney runs an office of more than 550 lawyers representing L.A. in all legal matters, including filing lawsuits and defending against them. Roy, backed by powerful progressives like U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, has vowed to take on the Trump administration in court.
Go deeper: Read more about the city attorney's role and what's on the table for Roy's first term.

Coyote becomes first mammal seen using 101 wildlife crossing: 'This is amazing'
Elly Yu
reports on early childhood. From housing to health, she covers issues facing the youngest Angelenos and their families.
Published November 5, 2026 at 4:57 PM PST
A coyote is seen early Thursday morning, the second sighting of the mammal using the wildlife crossing.
Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing via Facebook)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
The Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing over the 101 Freeway in Agoura Hills is set to officially open next month, but that hasn’t stopped some wildlife from already using it.
Cameras captured coyote footage twice — once last week and again on Thursday morning — making the mammal the first large animal species seen using the crossing.
“This is amazing — obviously, the wildlife are not waiting for our opening date,” said Beth Pratt, president of the Wildlife Crossing Fund. “The animals are already blessing this crossing and saying, ‘Yep, you got it right.’”
Construction of the expansive bridge began in 2022, aimed at giving wildlife safe passage between the Santa Monica Mountains and Simi Hills after years of research.
Pratt said it’s unclear whether the images of the coyote are of the same animal. The coyote in the most recent image from Thursday morning can be seen on the 101 structure holding a bone or a stick in its mouth.
“The coyote is validating that we got this designed right, and I think that there's something also about a coyote being first — kind of the L.A. mascot next to P-22,” Pratt said.
The National Park Service is installing more cameras along the crossing to document and study how animals use it. While images will be made publicly available, there will not be a livestream.
“We can't, for security reasons, because this is L.A., and if there's a mountain lion going across, somebody's gonna go try to pet it,” Pratt said.

Former clients of immigration lawyer Alexandra Lozano Kennedy can get free legal help in LA
Julia Barajas
is following the impact of President Trump's immigration policies on Southern California communities.
Published November 6, 2026 at 5:00 AM PST
An ad inside Alexandra Lozano Kennedy's now shuttered office in Commerce, CA.
Julia Barajas
LAist)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
The L.A. Law Library in downtown Los Angeles will host a free legal clinic this Saturday for individuals who believe they may have been victims of fraud or attorney misconduct as clients of Alexandra Lozano Kennedy or her law firm, La Luz del Camino Legal.
The former lawyer — who used social media and Latino religious iconography to attract clientele — had tens of thousands of clients and offices across the U.S., including one in the city of Commerce in Southeast L.A. County.
Until recently, Lozano Kennedy was licensed by the Washington State Bar Association, which enabled her to represent clients nationwide. Lozano Kennedy resigned in May and is now permanently barred from practicing law in that state. She was also suspended from practicing before the Department of Homeland Security, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services; immigration courts; and the Board of Immigration Appeals.
A lawsuit filed by nine of Lozano Kennedy’s former clients alleges that her firm filed baseless or fraudulent petitions for survivors of intimate partner violence and human trafficking. It also alleges that her firm placed client signatures on documents without their knowledge and that client declarations contained information they did not approve. She is also accused of using nonlawyers to perform client consultations and provide legal advice. Lozano Kennedy denies any wrongdoing.
The business cards that were distributed at Lozano Kennedy's firm in Commerce featured a prayer in Spanish on one side and an image of the Virgin of Guadalupe on the other.
Julia Barajas
LAist)
M. Lucero Ortiz, director of community legal services at Loyola Law School’s Immigrant Justice Clinic, said that, although USCIS informed Lozano Kennedy’s clients that they can withdraw their application or petition, the federal agency failed to explain the potential consequences of doing so.
USCIS could issue a Notice to Appear to people who withdraw their application or petition, Ortiz added. This means the agency could refer the person to immigration court, where they would have to defend themselves against being removed from the United States. While their cases play out, these petitioners and applicants could be subject to mandatory detention in an ICE facility.
Sponsored message
“Unfortunately, one of the strategies [employed by Lozano Kennedy] was that she did not give clients a copy of what was submitted to USCIS,” Ortiz said. As a result, many former clients don’t know what the agency is reviewing. It’s also “difficult for another attorney to assume legal responsibility or representation in those pending cases,” she said.
“For that reason,” Ortiz underscored, “it's very important that clients really take ownership of their own case.”
Loyola Law School’s Immigration Justice Clinic and Counsel for Justice, an L.A.-based nonprofit that provides legal assistance to underserved communities, will facilitate the workshop on Nov. 7, from 10 a.m. through 1:30 pm.
The volunteer attorneys, along with Department of Justice-accredited representatives, will provide free legal consultations. They will help former clients complete a change of address form to ensure they receive USCIS notices directly. Plus, to help former clients secure a copy of their case files, the attorneys will help them submit Freedom of Information Act records requests.
Ortiz encourages former clients to “bring all of the documents related to their interaction” with Lozano Kennedy’s firm to the workshop—including any texts or emails.
Because the former lawyer allegedly profited off of immigrant communities by casting herself as a miracle worker, Ortiz said she understands why her former clients might be reluctant to turn to another attorney.
“There is no financial incentive for us to provide these services,” she said. “Our main priority is to restore trust with the community.”
Sponsored message
How to register for the legal clinic
To register for the legal clinic on Saturday, Nov. 7, former Lozano Kennedy clients should email here.
The LA Law Library’s is at 301 W. 1st St., Los Angeles, CA 90012.
Patrons who arrive after 12:30 p.m. will be assisted on first-come, first-serve.

US Justice Department drops bid to force California to set aside disputed ballots
By Safiya Riddle | Associated Press
Published November 6, 2026 at 4:53 PM PST
Ballots are sorted the day after California’s primary election at the L.A. County Ballot Processing Center, June 3, 2026, in City of Industry.
Jae C. Hong
Associated Press)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
The U.S. Department of Justice on Friday moved to dismiss its own lawsuit that sought to stop California from counting roughly 20,000 ballots it alleged went to noncitizens until their immigration status could be verified.
The request to dismiss the case comes days after Republicans’ significant losses in the midterm elections and about a week before a scheduled hearing where a special master was slated to evaluate the accuracy of the list. California officials have previously said the list is out of date and includes legitimate voters — a sentiment that the federal judge presiding over the case echoed in his blistering order denying the federal government’s request.
The case was at the forefront of President Donald Trump’s administration’s effort to assert control over state-run elections across the country, which Trump has said are rife with illegal voting without providing evidence.
The Department of Justice remains enmeshed in litigation with multiple immigrant and voting rights groups seeking to limit its use of the list of what is says are suspected noncitizens. Another controversial suit it filed in Alaska at Trump’s direction before the election to block the victory of the Democrat in that state’s Senate race was swiftly dismissed by a federal judge. The administration is appealing that ruling but has yet to file a full brief at the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.
California had processed roughly 9 million ballots as of early Friday, with nearly 5 million still left to be counted, according to state election officials. The motion to dismiss the lawsuit said that, by the time of the upcoming hearing, the state will have already irreparably “commingled the challenged ballots with lawful ones.”
“The relief the United States sought and needed is no longer available—rendering voluntary dismissal necessary,” the motion said.
Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, previously argued in court that the lawsuit would be irrelevant after election day, because there would be no way to sequester the ones allegedly belonging to noncitizens. The lawsuit was filed in mid-October, when ballots had been sent to all of the state’s 23 million registered voters, and after hundreds of thousands of ballots were already processed. Once a ballot is processed, it is completely anonymized.
Sponsored message
Essayli said at the time the lawsuit was filed that his goal was to “safeguard the integrity of the election so it doesn’t have an effect on the upcoming election.”
“We want to stop the illegal voting. We don’t want to chase it later,” he said outside of court the week before the election.
California prosecutors in recent weeks have arrested over 30 noncitizens who are accused of illegally registering to vote. Some who were arrested were also accused of voting in previous elections. Elections clerks around California in the week before the election were sent subpoenas to testify before grand juries slated to convene in November. It’s not clear who is being criminally charged in those cases, but the department does not typically subpoena people whom it regards as targets of a criminal investigation to appear before a grand jury.
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter appointed the special master in late October, shortly after allowing California to proceed with elections as planned. Carter, who was appointed by former President Bill Clinton, argued in his blistering order that separating ballots at that late stage would risk disenfranchising citizens and warned it would “wreak havoc” on the midterm elections.
The special master would have also considered whether or not California election officials did in fact have a mechanism for separating the ballots.

Jared Bennett
is the watchdog correspondent covering immigration and law enforcement at LAist.
Published November 6, 2026 at 5:00 AM PST
Long Beach police officers responded to a report of a gunman stealing a van being repossessed just blocks from the Long Beach Police North Station in March 2025. That case has led to serious allegations about how the department handled information about one of the arresting officers at the scene that night.
Megan Garvey
LAist)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
Listen
0:41
Can the Long Beach police be trusted to disclose damaging information?
A filing this week by a prominent defense attorney accuses the Long Beach Police Department of a pattern of failing to uphold defendants’ constitutional right to a fair trial. Jared Bennett has the details.
Can Long Beach police be trusted to uphold the constitutional right to a fair trial? That’s the question raised in a new court filing by a prominent defense attorney, who alleges the department failed his client, Lonnie Jacobs, when it comes to ensuring basic due process rights.
At issue is a now-former Long Beach Police Department officer’s long-undisclosed conviction for an out-of-state assault.
In his filing Thursday, Scott Sanders, a defense attorney, outlines how the department hid an arrest and conviction involving one of its officers from defendants and the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office for seven years. Sanders’ filing makes the case that the LBPD’s failure to disclose that information for so long suggests the problem goes well beyond this case.
It’s unclear how many potential cases could be affected.
“The defense submits that the repeated and varied efforts by the LBPD at concealment and deception … reveal a department that simply cannot be trusted to meet its disclosure obligations,” Sanders wrote in a motion to dismiss a case against Jacobs.
It’s a potentially major allegation. The 1963 U.S. Supreme Court case Brady v. Maryland established that law enforcement — both prosecutors and investigating law enforcement working on behalf of the government — must turn over any information that could help the defense win its case. Failure to do so represents a violation of a defendant's right to due process and can result in mistrials or overturned convictions.
The Long Beach Police Department has not yet responded to a request for comment about this latest filing, but previously told LAist it complies with requirements under Brady.
Sponsored message
Greg Risling, a spokesperson for the Los Angeles District Attorney said the office believes their case against Jacobs can be proven beyond a reasonable doubt and plans to continue with the prosecution.
Risling said the office has discussed the disclosure issue with the Long Beach Police Department. “We emphasized the need to inform this office of all arrests and/or convictions of LBPD officers, even those which occur outside L.A. County,” Risling said. “They understand and agree.”
How we got here
Sanders, who exposed the consequential Orange County jailhouse informant scandal, was appointed to represent Jacobs by the court when felony charges were filed in May 2025.
Jacobs is facing up to four years in prison on charges that he brought a controlled substance into a jail.
Jacobs landed in jail after Erik Suarez, then a Long Beach police officer, arrested him in March 2025 on suspicion that he threatened a repo man with a gun. No charges were ever filed on that allegation, but Jacobs was taken to the sixth-floor jail at the Long Beach Police Department, where a jail staffer allegedly found a small bag of cocaine in his sock.
Sanders has argued the arrest that landed Jacobs in jail was based on misrepresentations and omissions of evidence from Suarez and another Long Beach police officer.
Sponsored message
Lonnie Jacobs in a still from a police body cam on the night of his arrest.
Long Beach Police Department
L.A. County Superior Court filing)
It wasn’t until Sanders attempted to subpoena Suarez, who left the Long Beach force in June 2026 and has since been hired by the Burbank Police Department, that the defense discovered he had been arrested in Cobb County, Georgia, in 2019 and convicted on battery charges in 2022.
What's next
Sanders is now asking the court to dismiss the case against Jacobs because not disclosing this information amounts to "outrageous governmental conduct” on the part of the Long Beach Police Department.
“One of the most important responsibilities placed upon law enforcement is that of disclosing evidence favorable and material to the defense,” Sanders wrote in the most recent motion, “and the willingness to do so even when said evidence is damaging to the credibility of one of its officers, hurts the chances of a successful prosecution, or damages a department’s reputation.”
The information is relevant under Brady, the filing said, because Suarez’s conduct in Georgia demonstrates “moral turpitude" — one of the standards that requires sharing information with defendants — that could be used to impeach him as a witness.
LAist has previously tried to reach Suarez twice by calling a phone number linked to him in public records. Each time, a man answered and said he was not Suarez, but that he was in contact with Suarez and had no interest in connecting him with a reporter.

Voters have chosen to increase LA's sales tax — here’s how it compares to other cities
Adolfo Guzman-Lopez
is an arts and general assignment reporter on LAist's Explore LA team.
Published November 6, 2026 at 5:00 AM PST
Watch for an increase in sales tax coming next year.
Matt Slocum
Getty Images)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
The city of L.A.'s current sales tax is 10.25%. But after the region’s stretched firefighting services became visible during the devastating 2025 fires, voters solidly approved Measure FD this week, increasing the rate to 10.75%.
It’s expected to raise nearly $350 million yearly for the L.A. Fire Department to hire more firefighters, purchase vehicles and upgrade fire stations.
How and when the increase will trickle down to you
It’s likely you won’t start paying the additional sales tax until spring. The exact date is difficult to predict: The measure says the tax will be collected on “the first day of the first calendar quarter commencing more than one hundred ten (110) days after the adoption of this Ordinance” by the L.A. City Council. The L.A. County Registrar-Recorder has until Dec. 3 to certify county elections.
Until then, the City of L.A.’s 10.25% sales tax won’t change. Then it will go up to 10.75%.
L.A.'s sales tax will go up to 10.75% after the passing of measure FD.
Julia Kozlov
Getty Images)
(It’s important to know that money doesn’t all go to the city. The state of California has a base sales tax of 7.25% to which cities add.)
Sponsored message
A $1,000 laptop, for example, would carry $102.50 in sales tax. But the sales tax increase would raise that sales tax by $5 on that computer.
Under state law, the municipal sales tax will be charged on merchandise such as furniture, giftware, toys, antiques, clothing and restaurant food.
Grocery food and medicine are exempt, however.
How L.A.’s increased sales tax compares to elsewhere
Highest:
11.75%: Palmdale and Lancaster (highest in the nation)
11.5%: Santa Fe Springs
11.25%: Azusa, Bell Gardens, Calabasas, City of Commerce, Compton, Covina, Culver City, Gardena, Glendora, Irwindale, Lynwood, Pico Rivera, San Marino, South Gate, Santa Monica
10.25%: Bell, Beverly Hills, Bradbury, Cerritos, City of Industry, Claremont, Diamond Bar, Hermosa Beach, Hidden Hills, La Habra Heights, La Mirada, Maywood, Palos Verdes Estates, Rancho Palos Verdes, Redondo Beach, Rolling Hills, Rolling Hills Estates, Rosemead, San Dimas, Santa Clarita, Walnut, West Covina, Westlake Village
Lowest:
7.75%: Tustin, Huntington Beach, San Clemente, San Juan Capistrano
7.25%: Thousand Oaks, Simi Valley, Camarillo
Outside of California:
10.4%: Seattle
10.5% : Chicago
8.25%: Dallas
8.875%: New York City
Next time you get sticker shock after you swipe your card or phone to pay for something, remember that cities turn around and use that money to pay for water, trash collection, police and emergency services with that money.

Trump replaces Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller as chief of staff after GOP’s midterm defeat
By Seung Min Kim | Associated Press
Published November 6, 2026 at 11:24 AM PST
L-R: Susie Wiles, Stephen Miller
Mandel NGAN/Alex Wong
AFP via Getty Images/Getty Images)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, mere days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections.
On his social media site, Trump praised Wiles and said she’d continue to work for his political organization. Wiles also released a social media statement Friday.
“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” Wiles said in a social media post shortly after Trump’s announcement. She added that her commitment to “the President and the mission” will not change.
Miller, long a key member of Trump’s inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies.
Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post.
Wiles’ departure comes almost immediately after the GOP’s midterm thrashing on Tuesday. She will be replaced by Miller, a longtime trusted aide to Trump.
The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026.
Sponsored message
Wiles is the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.
Miller is one of Trump’s closest and longest-serving advisers, jumping on board during his longshot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He currently serves as White House deputy chief of staff, and though he has a wide-ranging portfolio, Miller is most closely aligned with Trump’s immigration policy and rhetoric on immigration.
Miller is a former aide to hardliner former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., who would go on to serve as Trump’s first attorney general.
Wiles brought order to Trump’s campaign
The veteran Florida operative joined Trump’s team during his 2016 presidential bid to run the campaign in his adopted home state. She performed the same role again in 2020 before overseeing the entire 50-state effort in 2024. She is the second woman to lead Trump’s presidential campaign to victory, although she never embraced the formal title of campaign manager.
Wiles, 69, has been credited with steering the most disciplined of his three presidential bids, and Trump himself has said he was often told that Wiles led his “best-run campaign.” Often called the “ice maiden” by the president, she was seen as the no-brainer choice to serve as White House chief of staff at the start of his second term.
She cut her reputation as someone who brought discipline to the president’s chaotic style and shunned the spotlight, so much so that at Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.
Sponsored message
Wiles showed unusual candor in an interview
But in December 2025, nearing the end of Trump’s first year back as president, Wiles became the headline when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials conducted by the author Chris Whipple, an expert on White House chiefs of staff.
The Wiles interviews stuck out for their candor, which is unusual for a sitting White House chief of staff. She said Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality,” although the president does not drink, and said then-Attorney General Pam Bondi had “whiffed” in her handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files while remarking that Vice President JD Vance has been a “conspiracy theorist for about a decade.”
Trump and other administration aides rushed to defend Wiles, who in turn disparaged Vanity Fair for publishing what she called a “disingenuously framed hit piece,” although she did not deny making the comments that were attributed to her.
In the interviews, which were conducted over a period of several months, Wiles also revealed a bit of her management style, saying she was “not an enabler.”
“I try to be thoughtful about what I even engage in,” Wiles said. “I guess time will tell whether I’ve been effective.”
Trump grinded through four chiefs of staff in his first term: Reince Priebus, who Trump fired after just six months; John Kelly, who served the longest at 17 months; Mick Mulvaney, who held the role for a little over a year in an “acting” capacity; and Mark Meadows, who served as gatekeeper for the 10 months before Trump left office.
Sponsored message
Wiles overcomes personal health struggle
In March 2026, Wiles revealed she had been diagnosed with early stage breast cancer and she juggled surgery and treatments alongside her demanding job.
Six months later, she said she was “cancer-free,” indicating she no longer showed evidence of cancer after her pathology results came back clear. On social media, she thanked her family, friends, doctors and “everyone who prayed for me, checked in, and supported me along the way” and gave special thanks to Trump for his “unwavering support.”
“She’s tough,” Trump said of his chief of staff in an October 2026 event at the Whi
